summary: Presents three IETF YANG modules (ietf-ssh-common, ietf-ssh-client, ietf-ssh-server) plus a script used to build four supporting IANA modules. The client and server modules support configuring and monitoring Secure Shell endpoints, and the groupings can be reused by other models that use SSH.

plainLanguage.summary: SSH is a secret tunnel for controlling computers from far away. This gives a shared form for writing down how to set up each end of that tunnel, so many tools can fill out the same form.

subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for configuring the SSH client and SSH server inside any management data model.

tldr.problem: Many network management models need to configure an SSH client or server, and each would otherwise invent its own way to describe keys, trusted hosts, users and algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9644 defines three IETF YANG modules (ietf-ssh-common, ietf-ssh-client, ietf-ssh-server) with groupings that other models import, plus a script IANA uses to build four algorithm modules from its SSH registries.
tldr.outcome: Models for NETCONF and RESTCONF clients and servers can share one definition of SSH settings. The groupings cover only SSH itself, so ports and addresses come from a transport-level module such as RFC 9643.

today: RFC 9644 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Document Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9644 presents three IETF-defined YANG modules and a script used to create four supporting IANA modules. The three IETF modules are ietf-ssh-common, ietf-ssh-client and ietf-ssh-server. The client and server modules are the primary productions of the work: they support the configuration and monitoring of Secure Shell (SSH) clients and servers.

The modules define groupings, which are reusable chunks of a data model. They are meant to be imported by applications that need to configure SSH client and server protocol stacks. For example, they help define the data models for NETCONF over SSH clients and servers.

The text describes the modules as "generic", meaning "least common denominator" rather than "complete". Support for the basic SSH protocol of RFC 4252, RFC 4253 and RFC 4254 is included. Advanced features such as multiple channels are left to augmentations made by consuming modules.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a set of Lego bricks for building an SSH settings page. The bricks cover the basics, and anyone who needs fancier features can add their own pieces.

sections.title: Where These Modules Fit
sections.content:
The ssh groupings are one piece of a family of RFCs that together support configuring both clients and servers of the NETCONF and RESTCONF protocols. The RFC draws a dependency diagram with these labels: crypto-types (RFC 9640), truststore (RFC 9641), keystore (RFC 9642), tcp-client-server (RFC 9643), ssh-client-server (this document) and tls-client-server (RFC 9645).

The SSH groupings deliberately avoid transport-level configuration such as which ports to listen on or connect to. That is left to an underlying transport-level module, for instance the groupings in RFC 9643. This lets an application choose how the TCP connection is made. NETCONF Call Home (RFC 8071) is the RFC's example: it can use the ssh-server-grouping for the SSH parts and add its own TCP-level call-home nodes.

The modules also optionally support RFC 6187, which describes host keys and public keys based on X.509v3 certificates. The document states that it is compliant with the Network Management Datastore Architecture.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC handles only the SSH part of the setup. Another RFC handles the phone number and address, like one person writing the greeting and another dialing the call.

sections.title: Common Algorithm Settings
sections.content:
The ietf-ssh-common module holds what clients and servers share. Its transport-params-grouping lets a configuration list the SSH algorithms that are permitted, in four lists: host-key, key-exchange, encryption and mac. Each list is ordered by user, in decreasing order of preference.

The algorithm that appears first in the client list and also appears in the server list is the one used for the SSH transport layer connection. Restricting algorithms this way can help make a client or server compliant with security policies.

Algorithm names come from a union type. A value is either an enumeration from one of the four IANA-maintained modules or a locally defined string. Locally defined names must contain an at sign (@), following RFC 4250.

Four features gate the module's contents: ssh-x509-certs, transport-params, asymmetric-key-pair-generation and algorithm-discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a guest list ranked from favorite to least favorite. Both sides compare lists, and the first choice they both have is the one they use.

sections.title: Discovery and Key Generation
sections.content:
Beyond groupings, ietf-ssh-common defines two things a running system can expose. When the algorithm-discovery feature is implemented, a read-only supported-algorithms container reports which public key, encryption, key exchange and MAC algorithms the server supports.

When the asymmetric-key-pair-generation feature is implemented, a generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC asks the server to create a key pair. The request names an algorithm, optionally a number of bits, and how the private key should be encoded: cleartext, encrypted, or hidden. The reply either returns the key pair or, for a hidden key, a location.

The RFC's examples show a request for an ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 key whose private key is encrypted by a hidden key, and a reply carrying base64 placeholder values.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can tell you which secret handshakes it knows, and it can also make you a new lock-and-key pair when you ask.

sections.title: The Client and Server Groupings
sections.content:
The ssh-client-grouping has four parts. client-identity holds a username and the ways the client can authenticate: public-key, password, hostbased, none and an X.509 certificate, each enabled by a feature. server-authentication sets the trust anchors for checking the server: SSH host keys, CA certificates and end-entity certificates. transport-params reuses the common algorithm lists. keepalives is a presence container with max-wait and max-attempts for testing whether the server is still alive at the SSH protocol layer.

The ssh-server-grouping mirrors this. server-identity holds a list of host keys, each either a public key or a certificate. client-authentication can hold a list of local users, each with public keys, a hashed password, host-based keys or the none method, plus CA and end-entity certificates. It also has transport-params and keepalives.

Keys and trust anchors are not described here from scratch. The groupings pull them in from the keystore (RFC 9642) and truststore (RFC 9641) modules, so a key can be written inline or referenced from a keystore.

Neither module defines protocol-accessible nodes of its own. They define only groupings for other modules to instantiate.
sections.plainLanguage: The client form asks who you are and who you trust. The server form asks which ID card it shows and which visitors it lets in. Both forms also have a box to check that the other side is still awake.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The three IETF modules define groupings and will not be deployed as standalone modules, so their security implications depend on how other modules use them. Designers who import the groupings must do their own analysis.

The modules are meant to be reached through YANG management protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transports and mutual authentication. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM) restricts what each user may do.

In the client module, the cleartext client-identity/password node is sensitive to reads, so the NACM extension default-deny-all is applied to it. All writable nodes in the client and server modules have default-deny-write set, because changing a key, a trust anchor or keepalive settings can dramatically alter the security policy.

The generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC can return a private key in cleartext if that feature is enabled and the client asks. The RFC says it is NOT RECOMMENDED for private keys to pass the server's security perimeter.
sections.plainLanguage: Settings that could open the door to attackers are locked by default, and passwords are never handed back to people who just ask to look.

sections.title: The IANA Algorithm Modules
sections.content:
Four supporting modules are published by IANA, not by this RFC: iana-ssh-encryption-algs, iana-ssh-key-exchange-algs, iana-ssh-mac-algs and iana-ssh-public-key-algs. Each turns an IANA SSH algorithm registry into YANG enumerations.

Appendix A gives a Python script that IANA can use to generate the modules. New values must not be added to the YANG modules directly. They must be added to the matching registry in the Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Parameters registry group, and a new enum statement is then added to the module. The status substatement is included only if a registration has been deprecated or obsoleted.

The RFC also asks IANA to register URIs in the IETF XML registry and the module names in the YANG Module Names registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of allowed secret codes is kept by a librarian. A script copies the list into the form, so the form always matches the library's list.
